resources.string: You can set your own acceptable blur in the “Sharpness Criterion” menu. It is defined by the diameter of the Circle of Confusion (CoC). In Standard mode, the app calculates or selects this value from the frame format.
Exit hyperfocal mode and set the focus distance manually?
Depth of field: from %1$s to %3$s. Focus distance: %2$s.
Local storage is temporarily unavailable. Try again.
Calculates depth of field and where to focus for hyperfocal photography. Works offline.
Local settings could not be saved. Try again.
The smaller the acceptable blur, the smaller the calculated depth of field. Acceptable blur is defined by the diameter of the Circle of Confusion (CoC).
Traditional depth of field based on frame format.
Assess sharpness when magnifying a digital image.
Sharpness under the chosen print viewing conditions.
Set the circle of confusion manually.

Suitable for normal photo viewing without strong magnification. The app selects the acceptable blur — the Circle of Confusion (CoC) — from the frame format.

It first uses the value from the built-in catalogue. If none is available, the value is calculated from the frame diagonal.

This is a traditional photographic guide. It does not guarantee sharpness when inspecting individual pixels.

Helps assess sharpness when viewing a digital photograph at high magnification. Enter the resolution of the saved image in megapixels and the acceptable blur in pixels.

If the camera records only part of the frame, the profile must contain the dimensions of that area. The calculation assumes square pixels spread evenly across the entire frame area.

Real image detail also depends on the lens, image processing and diffraction. This criterion itself does not account for them.

Calculates depth of field for the chosen print size and viewing distance. Small amounts of blur are easier to see when the photograph is viewed up close.

“Fit” keeps the whole frame and leaves margins if needed. “Fill” covers the paper by cropping the photograph at its edges.

The visual criterion defines how small a blur is considered acceptable. A smaller value sets stricter sharpness requirements. Values of 1–3 arcminutes are guides for the calculation, not a guarantee of how every viewer will see the photograph.

File PPI and printer DPI help with print preparation but do not change the depth-of-field calculation.

Set how much blur you consider acceptable. Enter the diameter of the Circle of Confusion (CoC) in millimetres — a number greater than zero.\n\nThe value is saved without rounding and does not depend on the selected camera.

Choose “Fit” to keep the whole frame; the paper may have margins. Choose “Fill” to cover the whole paper; the photograph edges may be cropped. The app automatically matches the frame and print orientations.
The calculation could not be completed. Check the values you entered and the frame dimensions: numbers must be greater than zero. The app cannot calculate extremely large values.
Sharpness of the final physical image on a display.

Print-Based now takes into account the print size and the distance from which it will be viewed. Sharpness requirements are set by the visual criterion.\n\nFile PPI and printer DPI no longer affect the depth-of-field calculation. Your previous settings have not been deleted; they are saved in an archive.
You can leave these fields empty: they do not affect the sharpness calculation.\n\nPPI helps determine how many pixels the print file needs. DPI describes the number of printer dots.
Choose a suitable screen type and check its diagonal and resolution. The suggested values are examples; you can change them to match your device. The calculation assumes square pixels.
Use “Visual criterion” to assess the photograph at the chosen viewing distance. To set acceptable blur in display pixels, choose “Display Pixels”. The calculation uses only one of these methods.

A smaller value requires sharper detail and reduces the calculated depth of field.\n\nThis setting defines how small a blur is considered visible at the chosen viewing distance. It is measured in arcminutes and serves as a guide for the calculation, not a precise measure of human vision.
File for the full paper area: %1$s × %2$s px

The file dimensions shown cover the whole paper. With “Fit”, margins may take up part of the paper, so the photograph itself may be smaller. Its size is shown separately.\n\nPixel counts are rounded up. This information does not change the sharpness calculation.

Calculates depth of field for viewing the photograph on the selected screen. Enter its size and the viewing distance.

“Visual criterion” estimates which blur will be visible at that distance. If the screen size and proportions stay the same, increasing resolution alone does not make this criterion stricter. To calculate blur in display pixels, use the separate “Display Pixels” method.

“Fit” shows the whole photograph, while “Fill” may crop its edges. The calculation assumes square pixels and automatically matches the frame and screen orientations.

This is a guide for the selected viewing conditions. It does not guarantee the actual detail in the photograph.
The app cannot use this value in the calculation. Check the number and unit.

Fine details may become less sharp. This is the effect of diffraction: it becomes more noticeable as you stop down the aperture. A smaller aperture can still improve the overall impression of sharpness: greater depth of field may make the foreground and background look clearer.

Fine details may become noticeably less sharp because of diffraction. Stopping down further will strengthen this effect while also increasing depth of field. A clearer foreground and background may matter more than preserving the finest details.

Stopping down increases depth of field, but it can make fine details less sharp. The warning does not mean you must open the aperture: choose what matters most for your photograph.

For an approximate estimate, the app compares the size of the light spot formed by a point — the Airy disk — with the acceptable blur defined by the Circle of Confusion (CoC). Below a ratio of 1.0, there is no warning; from 1.0 up to but not including 1.5, the impact is considered possible; from 1.5, it is considered noticeable.

Diffraction increases gradually. These thresholds are guides, not an exact point at which a photograph becomes unsharp.
Diffraction estimate unavailable for the current input.
No diffraction warning at the selected criterion.
The app automatically shows the distance to focus at. It updates when you change the camera, sharpness criterion, focal length or aperture.
The right end of the slider sets optical infinity.
Depth of field based on recorded video resolution.

Calculates depth of field from the final video resolution and the acceptable blur in its pixels. It uses the recording resolution, not the number of pixels on the camera sensor.

In Auto mode, the app selects the largest central sensor area with the same proportions as the video. An additional crop makes this area smaller. If you know the recording area dimensions, you can enter them manually; the additional crop will then be ignored.

Width and height must follow the frame orientation in the camera profile. Square video pixels are assumed.

Camera video processing and lens quality can affect real image detail. This calculation does not account for them. You choose the acceptable blur.
A smaller value requires sharper detail and reduces the calculated depth of field. This setting is the acceptable blur size in pixels of the final video.

Set the additional video crop: 1× means no crop; 2× halves both the width and height of the area used.\n\nThe crop applies to the area already matched to the video proportions. This is not the camera crop factor relative to Full Frame. The lens focal length stays unchanged in the calculation.

Enter the width and height, in millimetres, of the sensor area used to record video. Keep width and height in the same order as in the camera profile.\n\nThe area must fit within the sensor and have the same proportions as the video. A difference of up to 0.1% is allowed for rounded dimensions. The additional crop does not apply here.
Manual area · additional crop is not applied
Enter a whole number of pixels, from 1 to 2147483647.
Set the acceptable blur in pixels. Enter a number greater than zero; decimal values are allowed.
Enter a crop factor of at least 1×. Use 1 if there is no additional crop.
Enter the recording area width and height in millimetres. Both numbers must be greater than zero.
The recording area is larger than the selected camera sensor. Check its width and height or switch to automatic area selection.
The recording area must have the same proportions as the video. Check its width and height or switch to automatic area selection.
The calculation needs the frame dimensions in millimetres. Enter them in the camera profile or select a camera that already has them.
These values are too large or too small for the app to calculate. Check the numbers and units.

The sharpness setting for this format is calculated automatically from the frame dimensions.\n\nThe acceptable blur — the Circle of Confusion (CoC) — is determined from the frame diagonal. The reference is the 36×24 mm format with a value of 0.030 mm.
Lens profile ignored. Standard values and app units are used.
Add and edit your lens kit in Camera Profile. Manual focal length and aperture input is always available.
Choose the units marked on this lens. If they differ from the app units, the current focus distance is also shown in the app units in parentheses.
Maximum Aperture at Wide End, f/
Maximum Aperture at Tele End, f/
Ignore Lens Profile, Show All Focal Lengths
Ignore Lens Profile, Show All Apertures
Quick-select buttons include all lenses saved for this camera. There is no need to switch between lenses. You can still enter any focal length and aperture manually.
Save the camera before adding lenses.
Check the zoom range: the first focal length must be smaller than the second. For a prime lens, turn off “Zoom Lens”.

Check “Minimum Aperture”: its f-number must be greater than or equal to the maximum aperture f-number. For a zoom lens, compare it with both values. For example, a lens with a maximum aperture of f/4 can have a minimum aperture of f/16, but not f/2.

At high magnifications, this estimate may be less accurate. In these conditions, the lens may behave as though the aperture were stopped down further. The app uses the f-number you entered and does not adjust it for magnification.
Use the displayed depth of field as a guide. At close distances, the calculation may be less accurate: real lenses do not always behave as the simplified model assumes.

At this distance, the app cannot reliably estimate magnification. You may be shooting in the macro range. A real lens can focus at such a distance, but it is beyond the limits of the simplified model.

Treat magnification and depth of field at close distances as guides. The actual result depends on the lens design and any additional optics.

The app estimates magnification from the focal length you entered and the distance from the sensor or film plane to the subject. It uses a simplified model for magnifications up to 1:1 — when the image of the subject on the sensor is the same size as the subject itself.

The optical characteristics of real lenses can change as they focus. Extension tubes, bellows and additional lenses also affect the result.

If the distance is less than four focal lengths, the model cannot determine magnification. This is a limitation of the calculation, not a restriction on photography. The depth-of-field calculation remains a useful guide.
The selected lens has a distance scale in feet. Hyperfocal distance is shown in both app units and feet so you can set it using the scale on your lens.
The selected lens has a distance scale in meters. Hyperfocal distance is shown in both app units and meters so you can set it using the scale on your lens.
